speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Our temperature was hitting the low 20 degree Celsius and there were also a few flash floods from heavy downpours.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I would expect during the hot months, it is going the other way and we will experience very hot weather.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Global warming, rising sea levels will affect all of us.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Yes, we have spoken a lot about climate change.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But there are areas where we are not doing enough.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We can still see callous throwing of rubbish at void decks and other public areas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We see litter from plastic bottles to just about anything being dumped into the drains, clogging the water flow, and causing the breeding of mosquitoes, rats, cockroaches and more.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, while one group is doing all the good things to save our environment, there is another group just senselessly undoing all the good work.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In Singapore, we may be too far away to realise the ice at the poles is melting away at a worrying rate.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is causing warmer weather and rising water.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Marine species affected by climate change include planktons, which form the basis of marine food chains – corals, fish, polar bears, walruses, seals, sea lions, penguins and seabirds.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And we must not think we can escape.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Most scientists believe that global warming will bring about a new era of extreme and unpredictable weather.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The impacts of climate change from rising temperatures, changes in precipitation, intensity of some extreme weather events, will have an impact on our health, too.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These will affect the food we eat, the water we drink, the air we breathe, and the weather we experience.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The website will give a list of suggested actions we can take to be greener.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have pledged myself and I hope you will join me.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is a good reminder of what we can do for the environment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope more Singaporeans will take responsibility for their environment this year.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Whether it is not littering or taking green actions, it all starts from a mindset change.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Let us pledge our climate action and persuade people around us to do so, and we can preserve the environment for future generations.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We should break the goal down at different levels.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And for an individual household, what are the goals to work towards?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Although there are rebates from 2019 to 2021, how will the Government help lower-income families cope beyond 2021?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How can we reach these households and give them easy, affordable ways to save electricity?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Energy saving is something that we should promote to all households.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps we can also look into how we can help lower-income families by providing them with energy saving bulbs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It would certainly be welcome by these families as it would cut down on their electricity bills.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry consider giving help to these families?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Do not just give vouchers or the bulbs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry go one step further, that is, install the bulbs for them with the help of some corporations?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: By doing so, the Ministry would know if the bulbs are installed or not, whether the bulbs could fit into old light fittings or not.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Otherwise, a good scheme may not get its maximum benefit because of implementation on the ground.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I want to touch on water conservation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We have done much in this area although I believe not all Singaporeans consciously show concern about water supply because there has not been a crisis to hit the message home.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It also did not help that we have a transient foreign workforce who may not appreciate the importance of water conservation for our city state.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I know we have the Water Efficiency Labelling Scheme which helps consumers to make informed choices when they buy products, such as taps, flushing cisterns, washing machines and more.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Retailers must put the new water efficiency labels on the products to help consumers make informed choices.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Our non-domestic sector also needs to look at how they can use water more efficiently.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I believe they are expected to contribute to our water demand growth.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share with us what are the initiatives that will be introduced to help businesses in managing their water demand and increasing their water efficiency?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore is one of the countries where we have taken commendable effort in controlling vehicular smoke emission.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, we are spared from the smog that we read about which occasionally engulfed the cities in several neighbouring countries.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am not sure if all motorists are aware that leaving their vehicle engines idling is an offence as I still receive feedback from residents very often.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Besides locally registered vehicles, we have an average of 20,000 foreign registered vehicles that enter Singapore daily.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can I ask for an update on what other measures the Ministry is taking to further control vehicular emission?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, let us grab the Year of Climate Action by the horns, though this year is the year of the dog.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, in the afternoon on 30 January this year, while I was having a meeting in Nee Soon, I heard unusual loud sounds of thunder.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Shortly after that, I started to receive Whatsapp messages and images from my grassroots leaders that quite a number of trees had fallen, a few fell onto vehicles while a few others were blocking road access.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: I went out to take a look at the situation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: I saw fallen trees and lamp posts, roads being blocked, slow traffic, panels of a covered linkway gave way.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: There were also many residents who had gone out to take a look at the situation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: In the midst of the chaos, I saw a touching Nee Soon "kampung spirit", with residents coming out to help clear the trees and looking out if anyone got injured.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: I went around to look at the situation and started to engage the agencies and residents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: A few mentioned that they have never experienced such an incident before, in terms of the extent of the damages.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: One Town Council staff shared with me that he had never witnessed such damages in his more than 30 years' work in estate maintenance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Others mentioned that Singapore's climate has changed, accompanied by worried expressions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: What role can businesses and the general public play in Singapore’s climate action plan?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: What is Singapore doing on the regional and global fronts to contribute to climate action on a larger scale?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: The Minister launched the Climate Action Pledge recently.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, as a low-lying nation, Singapore is particularly susceptible to the effects of anthropogenic climate change, chief amongst which is sea level rise.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is important to consider the impact of rising sea levels, not only beaches and sea walls but also (a) intertidal coral reef zones, (b) sand and mud flats, and (c) mangroves.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These zones are not only bio-diverse, but also provide ecosystem services, such as buffering from sea level rise.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Government confirm whether the study is looking into protecting these parts of our coastal sea level rise which are, themselves, sensitive to sea level rise?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In view of the fact that Singapore is not merely an island nation but also a nation of islands, is the study looking into coastal protection measures on our offshore islands, such as Pulau Tekong, Pulau Ubin and the Southern Islands?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are soft engineering approaches, such as planting coastal vegetation where they currently do not exist, being studied?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given that rainfall is a major hydrological input, is the Government taking these projections into account in its plans to mitigate floods in coastal areas?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, please take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The public was invited to pledge now to fight climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Schools and organisations were invited to join in as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Green groups were also invited to work alongside the Government to organise events and activities to raise awareness on climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This represented a strong effort by the Ministry to meet Singapore's Paris Commitment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: However, recently, due to public feedback, I raised a Parliamentary Question (PQ) on the Ministry of Trade and Industry's (MTI's) decision on the coal gasification plant on Jurong Island.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The public felt that the Government does not seem coordinated on our climate change commitments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As such, I would like to ask to what extent the Year of Climate Action is a whole-of-Government initiative with alignment from the other Ministries?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Has MEWR set certain targets to be fulfilled by each Ministry?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Furthermore, how are the various actions and initiatives under the Year of Climate Action measured in term of impact?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Next, I am heartened by the Ministry's bold action to implement the Carbon Tax encouraging companies to consider environmental, and not just financial costs in their business decisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The Carbon Tax is, undoubtedly, a milestone, an important pillar in our climate action.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Since its announcement, details on the carbon tax may not be fully understood by the public.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As such, can the Ministry share how the carbon tax will be implemented?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Our carbon tax price of $5 per tonne is significantly lower than that of other legislations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I understand our pro-business stance but this may not accurately reflect the price paid by the environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Could the Ministry share how they settled on that figure?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Furthermore, how did the Ministry opt for a Fixed Price Credit Based system, instead of a simple tax, or an Emission Trading System?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Next, with the impending implementation of the carbon tax and our move towards a low-carbon economy, companies may be concerned about difficulties in making the transition and increased business costs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The myth that a sustainable development is bad for a country’s economy should be dispelled.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It is estimated that meeting our climate change targets would generate additional investments worth $40 trillion globally by 2050.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Decoupling emissions from growth provides a golden opportunity to stimulate economic growth by boosting research and innovation and creating new jobs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In any case, all of us, including businesses, have a moral duty to safeguard the environment for the benefit of current and future generations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: To ensure the benefits of a low-carbon economy can be fully reaped at all levels, how is the Government intending to help companies in Singapore prepare for the carbon tax and transition towards sustainable development?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: So far, we know that it will affect the emitters of greenhouse gases, such as power stations.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Each emitter is different and various industries have their own sets of needs and challenges.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It might not be as easy for some industries to transit to clean energy.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Over the long run, we have to ponder if a carbon tax is the most effective way to incentivise industries to reduce their emissions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Circumstances have changed, and the desire of earlier generations of leaders to diversify our water sources has proved to be a boon many Singaporeans are thankful for.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The development of NEWater and desalination has contributed to this.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the pricing of such purification methods are not totally transparent to members of the public, unlike raw water.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the costs of these new methods of purification can be significant, I believe there is scope to share more details of pricing both upstream and downstream in order to drive home a message of the preciousness of water.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I acknowledge that sharing such information with the public requires accounting for the cost of upgrading and building transmission networks because the price of water is only one component while there are other costs, including research and development (R&D).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But that does not mean that it cannot be done.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such an approach will give members of the public greater understanding about why water tariffs need to rise and, hopefully, even moderate in future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Public Utilities Board's (PUB’s) water closet replacement project for flats built between 1987 and 1992 for residents in small flats on community assistance provides a foretaste of the significant opportunities available for a whole-of-Government approach to water conservation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A significant number of flats, for example, where toilets are completely renovated, can potentially host a variety of new water-saving features.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Ministry also consider if there is scope to improve, finetune or incentivise the Water Efficiency Labelling Scheme (WELS) with a view to nudge consumers to choose appliances with the highest number of ticks?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, if every drop is precious, can more be done to alter consumption patterns?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The opportunity provided by HDB upgrading may be a very useful entry point.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: One resident shared that her family members have to take turns to shower despite having two bathrooms in the flat.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: She said that when one bathroom is occupied, the other is unusable due to low water pressure.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I filed a PQ in 2015 asking PUB to consider setting a minimum pressure for the supply of water to individual HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Minister then replied that PUB is reviewing the issue.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It went on to say that setting a minimum pressure, I quote, "may result in fixtures not being able to achieve its water conservation objectives." Sir, the low water pressure problem only affects units on selected floors with gravity feed water supply.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Is the authority saying that we are only depending on these residents who happen to live on those floors to help achieve its water conservation objectives?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The rest of the floors are enjoying adequate water pressure.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Furthermore, setting a minimum water pressure does not mean people will waste water.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: There is a water valve outside each flat unit which the owner can adjust to control the water pressure to suit the needs of the household.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Last Saturday, on Singapore World Water Day, one of the pledges to save water is to take shorter showers.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: When water pressure is low, you end up taking a longer shower.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In an answer to my PQ in 2017, the national average water consumption for households for that year was 11% lower than a decade ago and about 60% of households consume less water than the national average.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I have been there a couple of times.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is a beautiful coastal city, and has a population of four million, is a world-class cosmopolitan city with a vibrant night life.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But this city is running out of water.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A month earlier, their daily allowance was at 87 litres.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The last water rationing in Singapore happened 53 years ago in 1963, during one of the worst droughts on record, when appeals to the public to conserve water fell on deaf ears.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the years since, we have become conditioned to the comforts of modern living.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Will they influence how the next wave of hike will take place this July?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Evidence suggests that the demand for water is relatively inelastic.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If the point of raising the water tariffs is to recover costs, then what we have done may be enough.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But if the point is to raise our awareness of the strategic value of water, we need to do more.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Should we have our "Day Zero" campaign to drive home these points and change behaviour?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, weather uncertainties caused by climate change could result in prolonged dry spells.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All of us would recall how the water level in the Linggiu Reservoir in Johor fell drastically in late 2016 and early 2017.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry share its strategy to boost the water supplies from our other three National Taps?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What investments and other measures does the Ministry have to enhance our water security and ensure that our water supply remains resilient to meet future demands and against climate change?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our second National Tap comprise our local reservoirs and storm water runoff.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the increasing number of extreme weather conditions, from prolonged dry weather to heavy downpours resulting in flooding here, storm water harvesting is an obvious solution.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Minister share an update on what infrastructure investments we will be making to collect water during the heavy rains while mitigating the flooding at the same time?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The other two National Taps are recycled water, NEWater and desalination.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are some of PUB's plans to further optimise used water management in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Minister share updates on the operations of our current plants and the progress of the building of new plants?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does the Ministry have plans to work with researchers to optimise the energy demands of desalination plants?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Last but not least, we must continue with our water conservation campaign.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must also empower our citizens and residents and businesses to conserve water.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on new water saving designs and installations in our buildings?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The non-domestic sector is expected to account for about 70% of the future water demand.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, it is critical that we work with this sector to optimise water conservation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What plans does the Ministry have to incentivise businesses to invest in water saving measures and technology?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not only do companies which use a lot of water be required to submit Water Efficiency Management Plans (WEMP), companies with significant usage could also do so.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there industry yardsticks by which companies can be compared against and assessed on their water usage efficiency?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If so, what are the plans the Ministry has for these companies which are not optimising their water usage?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore is moving towards becoming a Smart Nation and, increasingly, we will be leveraging technology to conserve and optimise the management of water.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Minister elaborate in what ways technology is being used or would be used to optimise the way the Ministry and PUB operate?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can such use of technology benefit Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In our homes, the four biggest uses of water are for showers, washing in the kitchen, laundry and flushing toilets.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How is the Ministry getting our households to leverage technology to conserve water for these household uses?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am interested in the updates for a couple of PUB programmes which tap upon technology to help households conserve water.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One is a trial by PUB to install smart water devices for 10,000 new homes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These devices provide real-time information on water consumption during showers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What has been the feedback on these devices and are the monitors effective in helping the families improve the management of their water consumption during showers?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If so, can these devices be made available to all households in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The second programme is a community project to replace the water closets in the homes of lower-income families with more efficient ones.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The replacements are expected to help them save up to 10% in their monthly water bills.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Has this project achieved its target of reducing the water bills of the selected families?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If so, would the Ministry consider expanding the scope of this project?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is it possible for PUB to mandate the installation of only water-efficient water closets island-wide?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How is the Ministry incentivising businesses and organisations to optimise water use through technological adoption?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Ministry give us some examples of firms which have successfully leveraged technology to cut water consumption?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is the area coverage of these sensors and how reliable are they?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is the average response time to the detection of leakages and how many more sensors will be installed?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Last but not least, would the Minister share how we are leveraging technology to optimise the production and management of recycled water, NEWater and further boost potable water supply from seawater desalination?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My constituency of Queenstown, which traditionally has been relatively safe from flooding, has in the past two to three years also experienced flash flooding more frequently.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What are PUB's plans to mitigate flash floods in the face of this challenge?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Minister share an update on the progress of the works on the Bukit Timah First Diversion Canal, which has been delayed by the difficult terrain, as well as the Stamford Diversion Canal and Stamford Detention Tank, which will protect our Orchard road shopping belt from flooding?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What are the main challenges faced in these improvement works and the building of retention tanks?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Is it expertise, is it manpower or component shortages?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry consider increasing the intake of foreign specialists and workers to expedite the completion of these tanks?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The new generation of pervious or permeable concrete has improved properties.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They are more porous and durable and facilitate drainage.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Does the Ministry intend to work with the other Boards or organisations, like the Land Transport Authority (LTA) or the National Parks Board (NParks), to use more of these materials in our roads and pavements?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also appreciate the Ministry's efforts to provide the public with timely alerts about flash floods through a wide range of communication channels, which include radio broadcasts, short message service (SMS) alerts and mobile apps, and LTA's Expressway Monitoring Advisory System (EMAS).

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For the National Environment Agency's (NEA's) SMS alerts, I would like to request for subscribers to be allowed to select more than one chosen location for alerts on the water level in monitored drains and canals.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would be useful for people who need to monitor multiple locations due to their travel patterns.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: The National Recycling programme was started in 2001 with the commingled blue bins.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: It was a good start to encourage Singaporeans to start recycling.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: However, as the recyclables are sorted out by the workers at the Material Recovery Facility and not by Singaporeans themselves when they recycle, is it time for us to up the game by progressively doing away with commingled blue bins and encourage Singaporeans to start sorting our own recyclables?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Key to the recycling effort also involves Singaporeans knowing what can and cannot be recycled and encouraging the knowledge and habit of sorting their own waste and unused items.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: In that sense, the recycling culture in Singapore lags behind some countries including Australia, Taiwan and Japan.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Waste management is typically perceived to be the responsibility of the Government.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: How can Singaporeans and businesses play a role in contributing to Singapore's vision of a zero-waste nation?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The Ministry mentioned last year that it is looking into a national e-waste management system.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: How about the recycling rate for non-household e-waste?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: We would need a comprehensive legislative framework and national collection infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: It is important to get the manufacturers, producers and importers of electrical and electronic goods involved in this process, so that we can work together to meet recycling targets.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Our market may be very small but we can still contribute to the movement for zero-waste manufacturing through a system of incentives and taxes.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: My constituency of Queenstown still has quite a large population of the karung guni men, and this informal sector, the rag-and-bone men of karang guni men could also be consulted and tapped upon in this new framework.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: I read recently about the rise of the new generation of karang guni men.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: These workers have had decades of experience and involvement in community recycling, going from door to door collecting from residents all over Singapore.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: They provide, and continue to provide, an important service and could continue to play a part in our recycling drive, especially as our population ages.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The Ministry may wish to consider a combination of incentives and fines to increase the level of cooperation from households.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: I hope that under the new framework, the set-up of collection points could be expedited.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The locations should be highly visible, accessible and convenient.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Are there plans to facilitate the recycling of larger items?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a problem that needs to be addressed urgently as e-waste pose both health and environmental problems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad that companies have stepped forward to promote the recycling of e-waste.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But this is clearly not going to solve the problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry mentioned last year that it is looking into a national e-waste management system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on the plans to manage e-waste and whether it can urgently establish a programme to ensure that e-waste is recycled or disposed of safely?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: They bear potential risks to marine life and human health by transferring persistent organic pollutants (POPs) up the food chains and into marine organisms which we may consume.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Some argue that microplastics themselves should be considered POPs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Is the Government studying microplastic prevalence in locally-sourced and imported fish, and the extent to which coastal activities like recreational sports and shipping contribute to microplastic prevalence in coastal areas?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Primary sources include microbeads used in the plastic industry and in care products like toothpaste and exfoliating facial washes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Will the Government consider imposing labelling requirements or a ban on industrially-produced microbeads as in the United States (US) and the United Kingdom (UK)?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What are the Government's plans to reduce overall plastic consumption, given that the secondary source of microplastics is the disintegration of larger plastics?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, 2018 has been declared as the year of climate action in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Plastic waste is the common type of waste disposed of at our incineration plants.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is well-known that single-use plastic disposables pose a serious environmental problem.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At present, more than 40 countries tax or limit the use of plastic bags.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Evidence shows that even modest policy interventions can have significant impact.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It may understandably be difficult to do away with plastic bags completely as we still need plastic carrier bags for everyday use like bagging our rubbish.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Countries which introduce charges for plastic carrier bags frequently have designated plastic refuse bags which people still have to pay for.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Prior to that, there is a progressive plan to make people pay for plastic products like plastic bags, straws, disposable food containers and disposable utensils in the interim.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MEWR has recently carried out a study of the lifecycle assessment of single-use carrier bags and disposable food packaging.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Minister share with the House its findings?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Ministry have any intention to roll out a progressive plan to reduce the use of plastic disposables in Singapore involving either the restriction or the banning of single-use plastic carrier bags, straws, disposable cups, containers and utensils?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Has the Ministry studied the recycling viability of biodegradable plastic carrier bags in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if they are viable, will the Government consider encouraging or requiring the use of such biodegradable plastic carrier bags?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, perhaps the Government may consider asking the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) FairPrice to take the lead in using biodegradable plastic carrier bags.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: These figures are alarming and calls for the introduction of a levy on the use of plastic bags to act as a disincentive to shoppers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Will NEA be imposing a plastic bag levy?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: How do they intend to reduce the excessive use of plastic bags in packaging?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: In Singapore, we are not doing too badly because we reuse plastic bags to bag household refuse and the waste is incinerated and not directly landfilled.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: As a result, the concern regarding non-biodegradability of plastic bag does not really affect us.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: In any case, the excessive usage of plastic bags is still undesirable and wastage should be kept as low as possible.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: NEA did a study on lifecycle assessment, cost and environmental impact of bags used in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Last year, I spoke on the food waste management and the eco digester centre in our Tampines hawker centre and Chong Cheng Primary School.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: NEA recently launched a two-year "love your food at school" project in some schools.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: First, in the long run, Singaporeans involved in the project will be more aware of the importance of food waste recycling.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Second, being part of the campaign also means consciously asking for smaller food portions if they are unable to consume much.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: There are also many places with canteens, such as army camps, prisons, the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) training centres and Home Team National Service (NS).

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: For example, in military camps, daily meals are catered for our servicemen, which include active personnel and those who are back for reservist training.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Some military camps also have canteens where servicemen could purchase food, notwithstanding the fact that meals have been catered for them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: As such, whichever food contractors in camps prepare food based on the weekly forecast of servicemen, it is inevitable that there will be food waste generated.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Therefore, perhaps a proper waste management system would be good.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Let us be more conscious of our food wastage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Deliveroo and Foodpanda are also investing in delivery-only kitchens to create and meet demand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is good news for the food and beverage (F&B) sector and consumers, but there are environmental costs and possible public health risks we need to tackle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The rapid growth of food delivery services in China have led to a crisis of mounting waste of food boxes, wooden chopsticks and plastic cutlery.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister share the results and implications of the study?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Further, is NEA monitoring the waste produced by the growing food delivery services?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, NEA regulates food caterers through licensing and publishes guidelines for consumers ordering catered food for events.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Catered food must come with a time stamp and delivered in hot boxes and insulated bags to minimise food poisoning risks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Food delivery services are now reaching a similar scale that could adversely affect public food safety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is the Ministry planning to regulate food delivery services in the same manner as food catering?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, since the Government's decision to resume building hawker centres in 2011, there have been concerted efforts by the Ministry, NEA and the hawker trade community to refresh and regenerate the hawker centre business.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hawker centres are an integral part our everyday lives.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It provides good and affordable food, common space for Singaporeans from all backgrounds to come together under one roof and it is very much a part of our national identity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Among others, how do we attract new entrants who are both passionate about the trade and see this as a viable profession?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How do we game-change the operating model so that we can improve overall productivity and keep operating costs low?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How do we inculcate gracious behaviour so that hawker centres will always be a pleasant place for all to dine and also, importantly, how do we ensure that the uniquely-Singapore culinary skills and tastes continue to be passed on?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I understand the Ministry and NEA have embarked on various efforts to rejuvenate the hawker centre scene.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Hawker Centre 3.0 Committee recommended to develop training opportunities and pathways for hawkers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can I ask the Minister how has the response been?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What have been done to improve the business operating environment for hawkers and to help the new entrants?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Improving productivity in hawker centres is a critical undertaking.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The aim is to address manpower constraints and to keep costs competitive.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can I ask how has the utilisation rate been like?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And how could we encourage more hawkers to tap on the grant to improve productivity?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hawker centres can be more than just a place for good food.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It can also be useful social spaces where we build a sense of community and belonging.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can NEA help inject more vibrancy into the hawker centres and encourage more fringe activities to be held at the hawker centres?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Have NEA done a review and what plans does NEA have to improve the tray return rates in the hawker centres?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, I am thankful that the hawker centre at my constituency will start construction this year and due for completion in 2020.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I welcome NEA to try out the various new initiatives at our soon-to-be-built hawker centre at Senja estate.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Early last year, the Hawker Centre 3.0 Committee submitted its recommendations to the Government with the view to improve hawker centres and promote the trade.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Keeping the hawker trade alive and vibrant is thus important although operating a hawker stall has its own challenges.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: In view of that, the proposal back then was to introduce a few ways to sustain the hawker trade and to support the injection of new blood.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Can the Ministry share what is the receptiveness of the public towards this programme, such as the number of people who enrolled or even dropped out along the way?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: As in any trade and sector, the need to be productive is important but costly.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Is it sufficiently utilised and how many have tapped on it?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Chairman, for several years, I have organised anti-littering exercises in my estate during the Clean and Green month.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The intent was to highlight to our residents the need to be responsible for our environment and to keep the estate clean.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But each year, the team of volunteers kept picking up more and more litter.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We found cigarette butts, used tissue, plastic bags, empty bottles, food containers, bottle caps and so on.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: One great source of irritation to many volunteers is dog poo left behind by pet owners who did not bother to pick up the dog poo.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Around my constituency, whenever there are any renovation works being carried out, I would also see plastic bottles left on the road by the workers of the contractors, plastic bags of drinks hanging by the trees and so on.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: To say the least, it is frustrating that the clean and green Singapore which I knew some years ago is no more.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Even the volunteers for the anti-littering exercises seem to have gone down in numbers as they felt frustrated at the lack of progress.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: With respect to NEA, it is not the number of summonses which we need to look at.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The question is whether NEA has been effective in reducing the litter which is thrown on the roads and other public areas.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Is NEA effective in keeping Singapore a clean city instead of a city which is being cleaned by our thousands of cleaners?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How do we stand as a clean city when we compare ourselves with the habits of the Taiwanese or the Japanese?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I would urge NEA to reconsider their entire programme of keeping Singapore clean.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This will help them understand the difficulties of the cleaner and also instill in them the discipline of keeping the environment clean.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sometimes, when I get residents who received summonses, they complained that they have low income and, therefore, cannot afford the fine.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, consider sending them for a mandatory CWO instead.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is to be fair to the rest of Singaporeans who take effort to keep their environment and Singapore clean.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Chairman, may I have your permission to distribute a handout to Members, and also to use slides to accompany my speech?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Since our Independence, Singapore has pursued sustainable development on a long-term basis, never compromising our environment for development or growth.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Erik Solheim, Executive Director of the United Nations (UN) Environment Programme, cited us as a model for other countries.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They resettled street vendors to hawker centres to clean up our streets.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They built rubbish chutes to handle our waste efficiently.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They planned carefully so that industries did not pollute our environment.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our Pioneers had the foresight and gumption to plan long term even if critical measures were difficult and unpopular.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Their steadfastness left us this liveable environment we enjoy today.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They laid the foundation for the next generation to build on.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our clean waterways allow us to harvest stormwater on a large scale.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our sewer networks join up through the Deep Tunnel Sewerage System (DTSS) to maximise NEWater production.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Because we have always processed our sewage for safe discharge, NEWater was possible on a national scale and cheaper to produce.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our hawker centres have evolved into vibrant social spaces.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Pneumatic systems will transform waste collection, where sanitation workers would not see our rubbish from end to end.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We can continue to be proud of our living environment.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I hosted 150 international environmental scientists and UN officials last month.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They were amazed by how Singapore can be an urban, clean and green city, all at the same time, and always looking new!

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: What our Pioneers bequeathed us has put us in good stead to tackle a bigger upcoming challenge: climate change.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is an existential issue for our planet.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Singapore is vulnerable, from rising sea levels to increasing rainfall intensities to longer dry spells.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I agree with Er Dr Lee Bee Wah that we need to take climate action now, for the sake of our next generation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: If the previous generation left us a clean and green city, we must make our legacy a sustainable city, as we pass on this treasured and precious land to our children.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We swung to the other extreme in the new year with a "January Singapore winter" and intense rainfall.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In February, high tides caused temporary flooding even without rain!

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: With rising sea levels, we could experience more of such phenomena.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As climate change cuts across various disciplines, the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Climate Change chaired by Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean and supported by the National Climate Change Secretariat ensures whole-of-Government coordination.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: All public sector agencies are committed to taking climate action in 2018 and beyond.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Government, however, cannot deal with climate change alone.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Everyone needs to join forces to reduce our carbon footprint.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is why Singapore designated 2018 as our Year of Climate Action.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We want to embed in Singapore’s DNA the instinct to care for the environment, like our national consciousness of conserving water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This will ensure that Singapore remains the best liveable city for our children and the best choice for companies to base their businesses because we have a successful climate action policy and an active citizenry.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We must ensure our policies enable Singapore to tackle climate change as we prepare for the future.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As a 17 February Economist article aptly puts it, and I quote "It is not droughts that cause cities to run out of water, it is bad policy".

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: All these will take time and, hence, we have started early.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These are large and long-term investments that must be premised on science.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Hence, in 2013, we set up the Centre for Climate Research Singapore to deepen research capabilities on the weather and climate of Singapore and Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Chairman, the Singapore Water Story is one where we strive for sustainability through long-term planning and investing ahead of our needs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This approach is more critical with climate change, where we need to grapple with both extremes of drought and flooding.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Last year, I spoke about the Netherlands and Singapore, two countries with different water stories: the Netherlands with too much water, and Singapore, too little.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This year, let me speak about Cape Town and Singapore, two cities with similar water stories which have taken very different paths.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As Mr Seah Kian Peng has said, since 2014, a three-year drought has pushed Cape Town's water system to the brink.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They are scrambling to build desalination plants starting from now.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Residents are bracing themselves for Day Zero, when their taps will be turned off and they are forced to queue to get their water rations.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For Singapore, there were concerns regarding Linggiu Reservoir, which supplements the flow of the Johor River, an important water source for both Singapore and Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But low rainfall, coupled with having to meet the abstraction needs of Malaysia and Singapore, depleted Linggiu to a historic low of 20% in October 2016, barely two years.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Saltwater intrusions and pollution required Linggiu to discharge frequently during such a critical period.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But the stock level can drop again quickly, and it has dropped in the last few weeks.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Should Linggiu Reservoir fail, it will pose major problems for both Malaysia and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Water is both a sensitive and strategic issue for the two countries.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is why it is often discussed when our two Prime Ministers meet.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: What Cape Town experienced is not a remote possibility for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We must not wait for a crisis to take action.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our forward planning ensured that in 2016, when Linggiu was at its lowest, we did not burden our people with water rationing when others had to.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The faith of businesses in our water supply was not eroded.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But the next dry weather event can come any time, and it could even be longer.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We must never believe that our problems are over.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about our used water plans.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: NEWater has allowed us to reuse water in an endless cycle and to keep the water within the system safe to drink.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Even with these investments, it does not mean that our water scarcity issue is resolved.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It only allows us to stave off temporary water shortages.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These sources are also energy-intensive and we do not want to be too energy-reliant in our drive to be weather-resilient.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is why PUB has always been exploring technologies to reduce energy consumption in desalination.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: There is promise in the use of electrochemical energy, waste heat and biomimicry.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But it will take time to realise these benefits.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For example, a carbon-constrained framework has prompted NEA and PUB to take a different approach when they were expanding their capacities.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They are looking at leveraging the interconnectedness of water, energy and waste to yield the best outcomes for the smallest carbon footprint.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The upcoming Deep Tunnel Sewerage System (DTSS) Phase 2 is not just a superhighway to transport used water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is a strategic infrastructure to boost our NEWater supply and water security.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: By combining the Tuas Water Reclamation Plant (TWRP) at the end of the DTSS and the Integrated Waste Management Facility (IWMF), the first in the world from ground up, we will employ the latest technology in combustion to synergise and maximise energy recovery.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Effluent water from wastewater treatment will be used for cooling waste incineration equipment, reducing potable water demand.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is equivalent to taking 42,500 cars off our roads.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As an added benefit, when DTSS is completed, we will have land savings of 214 football fields which we can give to the next generation to use.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Water is entwined with our nation’s survival and our everyday lives.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is not enough that the Government pumps billions of dollars into infrastructure to ensure supply.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The right pricing policy is needed to ensure good management of this precious resource.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We saw how subsidised water price led to high consumption in Cape Town, despite clear warnings of an impending water crisis.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Pricing is, hence, critical to manage both production and consumption.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It must allow for long-term investments and reflect the scarcity value of water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These principles shape our pricing policy, where we peg our water price to its Long-run Marginal Cost (LRMC).

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will actually have to pay it when we spend on infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Hence, we cannot subject the price of water to market distortions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: There are commercial sensitivities to the specifics of our pricing.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: By not revealing them, we ensure market competitiveness and the best possible bids in tenders.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Beyond market sensitivities, water is a matter of national security.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We must pay equal attention to water conservation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Prior to the drought, Cape Town was using 225 litres per person per day.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I said last year that with the permanent additional Utilities (U)-Save rebates, 1- and 2-roomers will not see an increase in water bills even after the full price revision.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: At this lower consumption rate, many 3-roomers will also not see an increase when the rebates are applied.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Water bills after the full price revision will still be within 1% of household incomes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The lower consumption, however, is not solely due to the water price.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our water conservation efforts like the mandatory water efficiency labelling scheme are bearing fruit.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Mr Seah Kian Peng and Mr Png Eng Huat asked about water conservation efforts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our water conservation efforts are yielding results because Singaporeans have a national consciousness to conserve water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As part of PUB’s comprehensive outreach programme, many schools are inculcating this consciousness in our children through education and water rationing exercises.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Similarly, Government agencies have committed to improve water efficiency by 5.1%, or 900,000 cubic metres a year, by 2020 under the Public Sector Sustainability Plan.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB started the water closet replacement project last year to help needy families save water with more efficient fittings.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This builds on HDB's HIP scheme, where participating households can replace their fittings with water-efficient ones.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB will continue to engage other eligible households.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Pritam Singh raised some suggestions on encouraging the take-up of water-efficient appliances, including offering rebates.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: According to PUB’s latest household water consumption study, more than half of the water fittings and appliances used by households are water-efficient models.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This high penetration indicates preference for water-efficient products, especially as the price difference between products of varying water efficiency ratings is insignificant.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB will continue to work with suppliers and retailers to introduce more water-efficient products.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As part of the Smart Nation push, we will also use technology to encourage behavioural change towards water conservation and enhance operational productivity.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB will be embarking on the Smart Shower Programme.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These devices provide real-time feedback on actual water consumption during showers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about the Automated Meter Reading (AMR) system.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB has been conducting trials on AMR systems, to replace current meters that have to be read manually.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: AMR meters can be read remotely and provide higher-resolution water consumption data.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Ms Jacqueline Chan’s family participated in PUB’s trial in June 2017.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Through a mobile app, the Chan family can track and take steps to reduce their daily water usage.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They have also saved about 8,000 litres of water after being alerted by their app to a leak in their water closet.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will explore how this system can be implemented nationwide.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The non-domestic sector must also play their part.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Companies can tap on the Water Efficiency Fund and the Industrial Water Solutions Demonstration Fund to support water-saving efforts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB is collaborating with industry to use the data collected through the Water Efficiency Management Plans to develop sectorial water efficiency benchmarks and best practices.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB has worked with the building sector, including offices, hotels and retail, to publish a best practices guide.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Growing and right-pricing our water supply go hand-in-hand with managing water demand.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The sum of all that we do will prepare us for the future.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For now, there is no need for national water rationing exercises.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: If we can get our policy right, we will avoid Day Zero.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Chairman, with climate change, Singaporeans will experience more frequent, intense rain storms.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked for an update on PUB’s plans to mitigate flash floods.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I gave a comprehensive reply in this House on 5 February.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB has set higher drainage standards since 2011, up to 45% capacity increase, but our drains cannot be built to accommodate every extreme rainfall event.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This would entail massive land take and much higher costs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have thus adopted a holistic source-pathway-receptor approach.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Work will commence at another 22 locations this year, adding to existing works at 73 locations.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As flash floods cannot be completely eliminated, we will help members of the public better cope by providing timely situation updates, including SMS alerts, about water levels.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Those who wish to receive alerts from more than one water level sensor can write in to PUB.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Over 70% of our coastline is protected by hard walls or stone embankments.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To protect against rising sea levels, we raised minimum reclamation levels by one metre in 2011, to at least four metres above mean sea level.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will build Changi Airport Terminal 5 at 5.5 metres above mean sea level.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To address Singapore’s long-term protection needs, BCA is conducting a Coastal Adaptation Study to recommend a national framework.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Scientists also worry about pest and vector problems escalating with climate change.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: However, we also observed a significant increase in mosquitoes caught in Gravitraps.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: While we continue with premises inspections, everyone can play their part by practising the five-Step Mozzie Wipe-out.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Climate change may worsen the spread of mosquito-borne diseases, such as Zika and Chikungunya.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are studying how male Wolbachia-carrying Aedes mosquitoes can be used to suppress the mosquito population.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will conduct further studies this year to strengthen our planning for an eventual suppression trial.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Climate change can also affect other vectors, such as rodents and houseflies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I encourage all to do our part by practising good everyday habits, such as disposing our food waste properly at home and returning our trays in hawker centres, to prevent pests in our homes and communities.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Chairman, besides climate adaptation, we also need to take mitigation action which is what we do to reduce emissions of greenhouse gases (GHGs).

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: One big focus is on energy efficiency for which we enhanced the Energy Conservation Act last year.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have more green buildings with more stringent standards in energy efficiency.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is what the car-lite policy will do.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: All these will reduce our fossil fuel use and carbon footprint.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Last year, I announced the new Vehicular Emissions Scheme to promote cleaner new vehicles.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: NEA enforces against smoky foreign vehicles at our checkpoints.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have tightened the turn-back limit since January this year.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: My Ministry is reviewing how to reduce vehicular pollution from older, more polluting vehicles.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will announce our recommendations in due course.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our industries can do more to mitigate climate change.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The carbon tax is the latest component of our wide-ranging mitigation measures.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui asked whether the carbon tax is the most effective way to reduce emissions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Pricing will encourage companies to evaluate opportunities to switch to more energy-efficient technologies and more sustainable processes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Recently, I spoke to Mr Jagadish, Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of SSMC, a semiconductor solutions company.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I was told that they are committed to a 30% reduction in GHG emissions in their process design.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As more companies, like SSMC, reduce their carbon footprint, whether through improved processes or when designing new investments, they also improve the Singapore brand premium and reputation for green practices.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Across the world, young people passionate about our planet will demand this as consumers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: An NEA poll showed that close to 70% of the public was supportive of a carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We aim to strike a balance between providing sufficient incentive for companies and Singaporeans to reduce their carbon emissions and giving them enough time to adjust.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our carbon tax will be applied uniformly without exemptions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Other overseas jurisdictions may have significant exemptions for particular sectors.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Hence, our starting tax rate cannot be directly compared with those of other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The carbon tax would apply to larger direct emitters – companies emitting 25 kilotonnes or more of GHG emissions a year.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will introduce a fixed-price credits-based (FPCB) system where companies will purchase and surrender credits to pay the carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The FPCB system is akin to a carbon tax, but it will allow us and companies to build capability to operate in a linked market with other carbon pricing jurisdictions if we decide to do so in future.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui asked about the tax revenue, while Mr Louis Ng asked about the Government’s support measures.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Minister for Finance has said he is prepared to spend more than what we collect in carbon tax in the first five years to support worthwhile projects.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked about the estimated impact of the carbon tax on households.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We expect it to be small, at about 1% of total electricity and gas expenses on average.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The additional U-Save rebates will help households adjust.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: My Ministry will also work with the community to help households reduce their energy consumption.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Senior Minister of State Dr Amy Khor will elaborate.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Chairman, organisations and companies have begun leading the charge.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The World Bank will stop financing upstream oil and gas projects from 2019.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I quote Mr Gan Seow Kee, Chairman and Managing Director for ExxonMobil Asia Pacific, that ExxonMobil "is committed to reducing GHG emissions in its operations, helping consumers reduce their emissions, and supporting research that leads to technology breakthroughs." Many firms, including many of our small and medium enterprises (SMEs), have made their climate action pledges on MEWR's webpage.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I am glad we are taking this journey together.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Striving towards a Zero Waste Nation is another key focus of the Year of Climate Action.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: A McKinsey study showed that to make one kilogramme (kg) of fabric, 23 kg of GHGs are produced!

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are running out of space to store our waste.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: If we continue business as usual, we will need a new landfill the size of three Gardens by the Bay every 35 years.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Waste does not magically disappear when we throw it down our rubbish chutes!

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui asked how Singaporeans and businesses can play a role in Singapore becoming a Zero Waste Nation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Government will lead in developing infrastructure and frameworks, including legislation where required.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Beyond legislation, our people, companies and civic organisations can demonstrate leadership with ground-up efforts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In Singapore, we have closed the water loop and achieved a circular economy in our water sector.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We should apply the circular economy to the waste sector.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The circular economy is also on the global agenda, where materials are reused and recycled for as long as possible.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As a CEO of an African non-government organisation (NGO) said: "There is no such thing as waste, until it is wasted." We will introduce the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) approach as a key strategy in waste and resource management.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Traditionally, producers are only concerned about the design, manufacture and use of their products.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Senior Minister of State Dr Amy Khor will share more details on setting up a national e-waste management system using the EPR approach.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As we strive to be a Zero Waste Nation, we will turn brown into gold as we engage in urban mining, as we recover treasure from trash, as we grow and transform a vibrant environmental services industry with good jobs for Singaporeans and, most important of all, as we build a sustainable and liveable home for our children.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: (In Malay):   The measures that are implemented to tackle climate change are taken on two fronts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: First, adaptation to cope with the impact of climate change.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will continue to invest billions of dollars in infrastructure, such as raising our coastal roads, building seawalls, enhancing storm-water systems and diversifying our water supply.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Besides climate adaptation, we also need to take mitigation action to reduce emissions of GHGs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: There are more green buildings with more stringent standards in energy efficiency.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have enhanced the public transport network and frozen the growth of our car population.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Last year, we announced the new Vehicular Emissions Scheme to promote the usage of new vehicles that are more environmentally-friendly.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: My Ministry is reviewing how to reduce pollution from older vehicles that produce more pollutants.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will announce our recommendations in due course.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The carbon tax is the latest component of the wide-ranging measures that we are undertaking to mitigate GHG emissions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It puts a price on carbon emissions to encourage the usage of technologies that are more energy-efficient and produce less carbon.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Environmentally-friendly practices should be a part of the Singapore brand premium.
