speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: (In English): Assoc Prof Faishal Ibrahim asked what Singapore is doing on the regional and global front for climate action.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has identified the fight against climate change as one of the top priorities for the UN and for the international community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In July, I will lead a delegation to the UN, where Singapore will undertake our first Voluntary National Review of the Sustainable Development Goals.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will use our ASEAN Chairmanship to galvanise support for climate action.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will share experiences and reaffirm the region’s commitment to climate action and the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will continue to plug ourselves into the global movement on climate change and work with partners to shape the international agenda.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As the saying goes, “If we are not at the table, we will be on the menu”.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To get a seat at the table, we must be credible.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This means that Singapore must fulfil our international obligations and show leadership on climate action.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Christiana Figueres, the former Executive Secretary of UNFCCC, said in an article published locally in Singapore in Business Times: "Fortunately, Singapore is attuned to this urgent turning point.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Its Year of Climate Action, backed by concrete steps in the domestic policy sphere, is the kind of leadership the region needs." Let me conclude.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To succeed in our climate action endeavour, the Government’s efforts alone will never be enough.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: All Singaporeans have a critical role to play.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Instead, Singaporeans must feel empowered to take climate action.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They should never have to face a water crisis like Cape Town.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I accompanied President Halimah for the launch of the Singapore World Water Day last Saturday.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: What struck me most was when two little girls, Alyssa and Abby, asked "What if this was our last drop?" Indeed, we must never let our children ask this, or “Why is our air so polluted?" or "Why is our sea level rising?” Our children are the reason why we need to take climate action – now.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I now hand it over to the Senior Minister of State Dr Amy Khor.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Chairman, in the Year of Climate Action, MEWR will rally everyone to take action against climate change, this year and beyond.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We hope all Singaporeans will join forces to ensure Singapore remains our best liveable home and a vibrant, sustainable city for generations to come.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Assoc Prof Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim asked what role businesses and the public can play in climate action.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: My Ministry will intensify engagement to galvanise action amongst NGOs, businesses, communities, households and individuals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: NGOs have always been passionate about sustainability, and many took the initiative to work together even before this year began.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will reinforce and support their ground-up efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I had a dialogue with NGOs in January this year, where we agreed that climate action collaboration and coordination across all stakeholders could be stronger.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: It will be chaired by Ms Cheam in her personal capacity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: MEWR will support this ground-up initiative and I have agreed to act as the Advisor.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will also be launching a Climate Action SG Grant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: NGOs and grassroots organisations can apply for this grant to defray some of the costs of organising programmes in support of the Year of Climate Action.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These companies recognise it is possible to do good and do well at the same time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We hope more companies will voluntarily pledge and take climate action.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: MEWR will support community efforts to educate the public about climate change and encourage climate action.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Grassroots organisations can apply for both the new Climate Action SG Grant and the existing 3P Partnership Fund from NEA for environmental programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will be launching a bulb replacement programme for 1- and 2-room HDB households to encourage the use of energy-efficient light bulbs to reduce energy use.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: NEA will also be organising an Energy-Saving Challenge this year to raise awareness about energy efficiency and conservation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Community engagement in climate action is a challenging long-term journey that goes beyond 2018, but we will stay the course to get every Singaporean on board.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Last year, I outlined Singapore's overall waste management strategy and the three waste streams we are most concerned about: e-waste, food waste and packaging waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As the Minister mentioned, we will focus on e-waste this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: That is like every person in Singapore throwing away 73 mobile phones every year!

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: E-waste contains heavy metals and hazardous substances that can seriously harm the environment and public health, if not properly handled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Some heavy metals can also be extracted from properly recovered e-waste and reused, which is more sustainable than mining for virgin materials.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked about the e-waste recycling rate for businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As Dr Chia shared, based on the results of an e-waste study by NEA, currently around 6% of residents place their e-waste in e-recycling bins.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We estimate the e-waste recycling rate by businesses to be higher, due to take-back arrangements that are usually in place between businesses, and manufacturers or importers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Chairman, with your permission, I would like to show some slides, please.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Mr Louis Ng asked for an update on our national e-waste management system.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Together, these products make up close to 90% of e-waste in Singapore and generally pose more harm to the environment if not properly treated.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our e-waste management system will adopt the EPR approach, which is also implemented in other countries like Sweden and South Korea.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They will be required to work with NEA-licensed Producer Responsibility Organisations (PROs), which will organise the collection, transport and proper treatment of e-waste, and help the manufacturers and importers achieve their targets.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, PROs will work with large electrical and electronic retailers to set up in-store e-waste collection points.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: All retailers must also provide free one-for-one take-back service for their products.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked about recycling larger e-waste items.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Apart from the take-back service provided by retailers, Town Councils also provide bulky waste disposal service, which will ensure collected e-waste is properly recycled.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will set collection targets in consultation with the industry and review them before implementing a penalty framework eventually.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The European Union (EU) started with an overall collection target of four kg per capita in 2003.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: After 13 years, the target reached 45% of all electronic products sold on the market by weight.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will study the practices in other countries to design a cost-effective system.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: By aggregating e-waste and enabling more efficient collection and processing, there will be greater value captured from e-waste, which is one of the more valuable waste streams.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This will help offset the cost of operating the e-waste system.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will consult relevant stakeholders to work out legislation and implementation details.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Some companies have already taken the initiative to implement voluntary e-waste management programmes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For instance, StarHub runs the REcycling Nation’s Electronic Waste (RENEW) programme in partnership with DHL Express and TES-AMM.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I am pleased to see retailers like Courts, Gain City and Harvey Norman coming on board the RENEW programme.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There will soon be e-waste collection bins in some of their outlets.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The mandatory e-waste system will help both the environment and the economy.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: EPR systems have generated new business opportunities and jobs in the e-waste management and recycling industries in other countries.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In France, for instance, more than 3,000 e-waste recycling jobs were created since EPR was implemented in 2005.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue to explore which food waste solution works best in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, around 90% of eligible stallholders participated in the food waste digester pilot at Ang Mo Kio, Block 628 hawker centre, which processed around one tonne of food waste a day for the past two years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Food waste digesters have also been installed in four of our new hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Digesters will be installed in two more hawker centres in Bedok this year, and in more hawker centres subsequently.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui asked how food waste in military camps and Home Team premises is managed.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To minimise food waste and food wastage, the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) and the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) use weekly forecasts of meals required to ensure that the right amount of food is prepared.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA works with both Ministries on food waste management initiatives, such as with the Central Manpower Base, on NEA's Food Wastage Reduction Outreach Programme.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Several army camps are also participating in NEA and PUB's food waste pilots, where source-segregated food waste is collected and transported to a demonstration facility at Ulu Pandan Water Reclamation Plant.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There, food waste is co-digested with used water sludge to generate biogas.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked about packaging waste produced by food delivery services.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: While NEA does not monitor this specifically, the total amount of packaging waste has remained fairly constant over the last few years and makes up around a third of the total domestic waste in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The voluntary Singapore Packaging Agreement (SPA) has cumulatively reduced almost 39,000 tonnes of packaging waste since its inception in 2007.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui and Mr Dennis Tan asked about our efforts to deal with plastic waste and, specifically, whether we will impose a charge or ban on single-use plastic bags.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Unlike many of the countries that have imposed a ban or mandatory charge on plastic bags, we do not directly landfill our plastic disposables but incinerate them.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Hence, we do not face the land and water pollution issues that plague those countries.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Plastic bags are also necessary for responsible and hygienic bagging of waste in our moist, tropical climate.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Unbagged household waste attract more pests like cockroaches and rats, creating serious environmental and health problems.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The study concluded that consumers can generally reduce their environmental impact by using reusable bags and food containers instead of disposables.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In Singapore, a more sustainable approach is to tackle the excessive consumption of all types of disposables.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will step up engagement with stakeholders to cut down on the excessive use of plastic bags as well as disposables like single-use food containers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, Foodpanda is working on a trial where customers can opt out of disposable cutleries when ordering food.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Zero Waste Singapore also launch an innovative Bring Your Own (BYO) Singapore campaign last year to incentivise consumers to bring their own reusable bags or containers to eateries and supermarkets to earn discounts or free gifts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue to support such efforts while holistically tackling the broader issue upstream by reducing all types of packaging waste at source.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Leon Perera also spoke about microplastics, an issue receiving increasing international attention, which we are working on closely with our international partners.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To ensure that Singapore does not contribute to marine litter and microplastics, we have stringent and comprehensive regulations to control pollution and manage waste.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We enforce strict anti-littering laws and incinerate our waste and conduct cleanups of waterways and beaches to minimise marine litter.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our island is also fully sewered and all used water is collected and treated to international standards before discharge.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: During used water treatment, microbeads, a form of microplastics, will be substantially removed as sludge and disposed of by incineration.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition, the Agri-Food and Veterinary Authority (AVA) conducts regular food safety tests on locally-sourced as well as imported fish.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: During these tests, AVA monitors for chemical contaminants found in microplastics, which may affect the safety of the fish for consumption.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: AVA will continue to monitor this issue and introduce appropriate food safety measures, where necessary.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We agree with Mr Lim Biow Chuan that it is important to keep Singapore clean and we couple education with enforcement measures to tackle littering.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Generally, more callous littering offenders would be more culpable and liable for stiffer penalties.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: CWO, which is issued by the Court, is meant for more severe cases like recalcitrant litterbugs, and it would be excessive to impose on all littering offenders.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan may also wish to know that foreign workers convicted and fined more than $2,000 or jailed for littering-related offences may have their work passes revoked and banned from employment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Public Hygiene Council (PHC) has been working alongside the Singapore Kindness Movement (SKM), to promote the values of picking up after ourselves and keeping our environment clean.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It is not sustainable to keep intensifying enforcement against littering.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Instead, everyone should take ownership of the cleanliness of their homes and communities, and I hope that everyone can join us in our efforts to keep Singapore clean and litter-free.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked if we have plans to regulate new food delivery service providers like Foodpanda and UberEats in the same manner as food caterers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Unlike food caterers, food delivery service providers are not involved in the preparation of food.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Food catering involves the advance preparation of large quantities of food at the premises of consumers, while food delivery service providers generally transport smaller quantities of food from various eateries to customers for immediate consumption.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These service providers, therefore, do not pose the same level of risk as caterers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Food delivery service providers do have the responsibility to ensure that delivered food is not contaminated during delivery, and that the interiors of their delivery vehicles are clean and free of pests.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Failure to do so is an offence under the Environmental Public Health Act.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: If there is food poisoning arising from malpractice during delivery, such as if the delivery person mishandles or deliberately tampers with the food, the delivery person can also be charged for possessing food which is unclean or unfit for consumption.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will, however, continue monitoring the industry closely and, if necessary, tighten food hygiene requirements to maintain high food safety standards.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Chairman, many Singaporeans have told me that hawker centres and the food they offer are what they identify with and miss most when they are overseas.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Government has invested significantly in developing and enhancing hawker centres over the years to ensure that we and future generations can continue to enjoy our unique hawker culture.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To achieve this, hawker centres undergo cyclical repair and redecoration works about once every seven years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These naturally-ventilated centres have better layout with wider stall fronts, larger circulation spaces, family seating areas with lower tables for young children, and even spaces for performances and other community activities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The remaining new hawker centres will be built in areas like Sembawang, Sengkang, Punggol, Bukit Panjang North and Bukit Batok in the coming years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue improving the design of our hawker centres as we develop new ones and renovate existing ones to meet the changing needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Besides hardware, we also continually seek new ideas to better manage our hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: One way we are doing this is by implementing alternative management models for new hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have appointed socially-conscious operators to manage our new hawker centres, tapping on their experience managing other F&B operations to enhance the dining experience for patrons.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They introduce new concepts and ideas and improve operational efficiency while ensuring affordability of food.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These operators must also monitor food prices at their centres to prevent unreasonable price hikes, and ensure hawkers offer at least a few affordable entry-level meals.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We must also sustain the hawker trade by both attracting new entrants and supporting existing hawkers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Government accepted the Hawker Centre 3.0 (HC 3.0) Committee's recommendations last year, which focused on addressing hawkers' manpower constraints, reducing their workload and improving productivity.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui and Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked about the progress of these recommendations.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I am pleased to say that we have made significant progress.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have opened up training opportunities and pathways for aspiring hawkers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA collaborated with the People’s Association (PA) to successfully launch the first season of the Hawker Fare Series of culinary classes for close to 100 participants from May to August last year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The second season has already started this year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA and the Institute of Technical Education (ITE) also jointly developed an “Introduction to Managing a Hawker Business” course, and more than 100 students participated in the inaugural class last year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Four more classes will be held this year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Two weeks ago, we launched the Incubation Stall Programme to give aspiring hawkers a chance to try out as a hawker.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have offered 13 incubation stalls in hawker centres across the island.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Three stalls have been taken up so far, with another three applications received.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This includes stall-level initiatives, like the Hawkers’ Productivity Grant (HPG), launched last year to promote greater use of kitchen automation equipment and help hawkers overcome manpower constraints and reduce their workload through greater productivity.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Fifty-eight hawkers have been awarded this Grant as of last month, such as Mr Tay Chen Boon, a 74-year-old hawker who has been selling popiah at Block 93 Lorong 4 Toa Payoh for the past 45 years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: His new continuous feed vegetable cutter saves him almost two hours of preparation time daily, as he does not have to cut the vegetables by hand.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: At the centre-level, the Government has funded initiatives like automated tray return systems (ATRS) and centralised dishwashing (CDW) services in existing hawker centres undergoing renovation.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So far, we have introduced these initiatives to two existing hawker centres, working with the Hawkers’ Associations.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We intend to roll out these systems in phases to up to 25 existing hawker centres over the next few years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We thank Mr Liang Eng Hwa for expressing his support for these new initiatives at his upcoming hawker centre in Senja.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These centre-level initiatives allow hawkers to focus on preparing and cooking their food, saving them time spent collecting and washing crockery or employing someone to do so.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They also do not have to invest in the crockery as these are provided by the centralised dishwashing vendor.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Taken together, these savings should offset the fees they pay for centralised dishwashing services.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Government also co-funds up to 70% of the operating costs of the initiatives for two years, to lower the initial adoption cost.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This also benefits hawkers as faster turnover means they can serve more patrons.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Removing leftover food from the table addresses the bird nuisance issue and creates a cleaner, more hygienic dining environment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Returning trays with used crockery after meals is a small gesture of consideration for the next diner.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Some people have said encouraging tray return deprives cleaners of their job.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Cleaners are not going to lose their jobs just because we become more considerate and return our trays.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Cleaning is not an easy job that attracts many, especially locals.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Cleaning companies cannot hire enough cleaners and existing cleaners have difficulties coping with clearing crockery and cleaning the tables, particularly during peak hours.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: By returning our own trays, we allow cleaners to focus on cleaning tables, improving productivity as well as the quality of their jobs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are trying various ways to improve our tray return rates.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Under this project, cleaners encourage patrons to clear their own trays after meals, and they wear aprons displaying a message reminding patrons to return their trays.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There are also posters on the tables with similar messages.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The results at both hawker centres have been encouraging.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These initiatives benefited cleaners at these centres, like 65-year-old Mdm Chin, a cleaner at Adam Food Centre who said she could concentrate on cleaning tables, making her job easier.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have also piloted an ATRS with a deposit system at two of our existing hawker centres to "nudge" patrons to return their trays.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We hope that, over the longer term, there is no need to have such a system, after tray return becomes second nature.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In the meantime, we also plan to introduce behavioural nudges and cues at these two hawker centres to further reinforce the message.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Chairman, may I have your permission to speak in Mandarin.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: (In Mandarin):   The Government has continually upgraded and improved hawker centres in terms of the design of the facilities, the way they are run and the approach to tendering stalls.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is done so that everyone can benefit as diners can enjoy affordable food, while stall holders have a clean working environment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We also introduced productivity initiatives, such as CDW and ATRS, to help the stallholders address their manpower issues and reduce their workload.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They do not take away work from the cleaners but actually make their work easier so that they can focus on cleaning tables, improving their productivity.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Diners also benefit as they can access clean tables quickly, and enjoy a more pleasant, hygienic dining environment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: All these initiatives ultimately benefit all Singaporeans – diners, cleaners, as well as the stallholders.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: (In English): Another recommendation of HC 3.0 relates to enhancing the vibrancy of our hawker centres as social spaces.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA launched the "Vibrant Hawker Centres" programme last June to encourage individuals, teams, organisations or institutions to organise regular activities at hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Hawker centres will continue to prosper as a key part of our social fabric, if everyone plays their part – hawkers, private operators, and patrons like you and I.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Together, we can continue enjoying tasty local food in our beloved hawker centres for years to come.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Chairman, to paraphrase the Minister for Finance’s words during the Budget Debate, when he was referring to Reserves: "We are stewards of our environment, just like Reserves, preserving and enhancing it for ourselves and for future generations, just as our forefathers had done for us." Everyone can play a part and benefit from Climate Action.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We hope that what we do collectively helps reverse the global tragedy of the commons and ensures Singapore’s development remains on a sustainable path.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And for a start, I hope that all Members of this House, besides Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Assoc Prof Muhammad Faishal, can lead by example and take the Climate Action Pledge online, and encourage your friends, families and constituents to do so.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I can send you the quick response (QR) code if you wish, so that you can take the pledge.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Together, we can build a liveable and sustainable environment now and into the future!

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Is there a plan to get the corporation to come in to help?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: And for those cases where the bulb does not fit into the old light fitting, is there a plan to change the light fittings?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: I have four covered basketball courts in Khatib where basketballers from all over Singapore come every day to enjoy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: However, at the end of the day, it looks like a war zone.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: How will the Ministry help in fighting this littering issue?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Can we use gadgets, modern technology, to nab the culprits?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They can provide convenient door-to-door collection of the used appliances and, where it cannot be reused, then they can actually send it to the recyclers through the PROs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, we will work closely with the grassroots to do this.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But at the end of the day, we need to ensure that people take ownership of the environment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: If they use the courts, then they must take ownership and prevent littering.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, some kind of administrative process should be implemented so that we can identify who are the ones who are using the courts, too.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: First, I am delighted that our per capita water usage has just gone down to 143 litres a day.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: My second clarification is: the Minister mentioned that if we get our policies right, there is no need for a Day Zero campaign.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: My question is: having a campaign, having a water rationing exercise island-wide, would this not nudge us, bring the entire population towards this goal and, in the process, also build our water, physical or mental resilience?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: So, I see a lot more benefits, I do not see any downside.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: So, I would urge the Minister to review this decision.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I am glad it is going down, and what we would like to see is that it will go down sustainably and not just episodically.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, over the next one or two years, we will watch this figure.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will put in water conservation efforts to help our residents, our citizens, to save water and then look at whether we need to revise it one or two years down the line.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But certainly, there is a lot of scope for us to put in technologies, to put in measures that will, hopefully, get us better than 140 litres per day, as we targeted.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Now, a lot more schools have come on board.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And even as we try to do this at both the primary and secondary schools, there are issues in ensuring that it is safe.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Basic hygiene is still something we want to ensure, particularly the aged, and, in this case, they are very young.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Let us go through that exercise and then, over time, not make a water ration exercise become a disaster for individuals.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, for the moment, let us just do this at the school level first and, over time, if there is ever a need for us to have that national consciousness tilt up again, probably we will need to do that.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Chairman, I have just got a question for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: And the low pressure that is experienced by households affects only certain households on certain levels of an HDB block.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: So, for PUB to cite water conservation objective as a reason for not setting a minimum water pressure, to these affected households, it is a bit unfair because everyone else in the block is enjoying good water pressure.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: So, would the Minister be doing something about this or would be reviewing this?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The professional bodies, PUB as well as the industry, came together after the Member raised this issue in 2015 to actually see whether they need to revise the Code of Practice for Water Services (CP)48 to see whether we should actually put a minimum level.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Water conservation issue is only one of them.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is just not sound engineering-wise, and let the professional engineer (PE) set it out, design it at the start, and make sure it is right.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As a former Town Council Chairman, I have addressed some of these issues in the households who complained about the water pressure, and it can be done.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: You have to work with PUB, work with plumbers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Sometimes, it is a problem inside, sometimes it is a problem outside, sometimes it is the booster pump.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: There are many issues that we can try to address for the residents individually.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: I just wanted to ask the Senior Minister of State whether she thinks that the state of cleanliness in Singapore, is it better today compared to five years ago?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Second clarification: why does NEA feel that issuing a CWO is a more serious offence as compared to imposing a fine?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: When you impose a fine on a litterbug, he pays the fine, five minutes later, he forgets about it, but he walks away complaining that the Government is trying to make money out of him.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: But if you impose a CWO on a litterbug, you take one hour away from him, make him pick up litter, he will realise better the effect of the litter that other litterbugs have thrown on the ground, and the lesson will stay with him for a much longer period of time and, hopefully, that will deter him from littering again.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I am also pleased that he is extremely passionate about keeping Singapore clean.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Asking me whether I think Singapore is cleaner now or not, I may not be the right person to ask.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We had done a public cleanliness perception survey between late 2016 and early 2017 with 2,000 respondents.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But it is a properly done survey, 2,000 respondents, 82%.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But, of course, their satisfaction with different areas varies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, they were most satisfied, for instance, with transport nodes, Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) stations and so on.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They ranked that as they were most satisfied in terms of cleanliness.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Areas where they were not satisfied with, which I think we all have some idea of, would be like HDB void decks, F&B establishments, that is, the eating establishments, as well as places after public events.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA does work on having more enforcement, for instance, at hot spot areas, and also getting volunteers to turn these hot spot areas into Bright Spots.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to the efficacy, for instance, of enforcement, as I have said, we couple enforcement as a deterrence with education, and I agree with the Member that we need to start young, from schools.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And that is what the Public Hygiene Council and Singapore Kindness Movement have done.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As regards why not CWO on everyone, we also need to realise that there may be people who, for medical reasons, cannot do CWOs, for instance.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: CWO is actually harsher because, if it is a fine, they just pay.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But CWO, they all have to take leave, they will have to go and do their CWO, and it may be in public places where they do not want to be seen.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I do not believe he touched on this particularly, but could he confirm if the study is also looking at parts of the coast, like intertidal coral reef zones, sands and mudflats and mangroves, as well as the islands like Pulau Tekong, Pulau Ubin and the Southern Islands?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Look at the climate change impact on those areas as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The second question is: are soft engineering approaches, such as planting coastal vegetation, if they do not exist right now, also being studied as part of MEWR's plans?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, the consideration will need to be made when we reinforce or increase the coastal protection that we will have to do over the years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It has been proven effective in other countries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It has resulted in the reduction of the use of plastic bags, which is exactly what MEWR's role is.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: So, I want to stress that we should look into that further and to stress also that this is not a ban on the use of plastic bags.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: If not, does MEWR intend to collect such data so that we can measure the effectiveness of the current retailers' schemes?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As I have said, the lifecycle assessment study did show that for plastic bags, it has got the highest GHG emissions and energy used.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But on the other hand, other disposable bags, for instance, biodegradable bags which are so-called more eco-friendly, also actually have some environmental impact in terms of production.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Paper bags require lots of water to produce and, of course, there is this issue of land deforestation.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have to plant trees to produce paper pulp and so on.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Another example with the oxo-biodegradable bag which actually is made of plastic additives that will help to accelerate the degradation of the bag and that is supposed to be more eco-friendly.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But actually, because we incinerate our waste, including plastic, these oxo-biodegradable bags will still have the same environmental impact as plastic bags.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: If we actually place a charge or ban, where we have a ban on bags, what will happen is that there will be substitutes for using other bags.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, what we are saying is that because we incinerate waste, we do not have the same issue as many of these other countries which actually land fill directly.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But we agree that we should curb or tackle the issue of excessive use of such plastic bags and other disposables.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Just a quick one for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Could I just ask or clarify whether it is possible for someone who has been caught for littering, if he is unable to pay the fine, could he choose to take a CWO instead of paying a fine?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: If they are first offenders and they cannot pay the fine, we will look at various ways to assist if we can.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Would the mover wish to withdraw the amendment?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: And to all in this House, I would like to urge Members to take the climate action pledge if you have not done so.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Let us take positive action to save the earth for our next generation.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
